Base directory for this skill: /Users/marlin/.claude/skills/cross-review

# Cross-model code review

A model reviewing its own output is a weak check: it repeats the assumptions it
made while writing. This skill breaks that loop by routing every slice of a diff
to the model that **didn't** write it.

```
diff ──┬─ Claude-authored ──────────► codex exec      (OpenAI reviews Anthropic)
       ├─ Codex-authored ───────────► claude -p       (Anthropic reviews OpenAI)
       └─ human / unattributable ───► codex exec      (opposite of this session)
              each side × N lenses         │
                                           ▼
                                   merged + deduped findings
                                           │
                                           ▼
                          verify.py: one throwaway worktree per finding,
                          reproduce it by RUNNING code (not the raiser,
                          not the author) ──► reproduced / refuted / inconclusive
                                           │
                                           ▼
                                   you fix ──► record.py (next run learns)
```

Reviewers run **concurrently** and **read-only**; verification runs in
disposable git worktrees that never touch the real repo. You (the session agent)
own the fixes and the report.

## Preflight

1. **Both CLIs must be present.** `codex --version` and `claude --version`. If
   `codex` is missing, tell the user to install and sign in — don't do it
   yourself:
   > Codex CLI isn't installed. Install with `npm i -g @openai/codex`, then sign
   > in with `codex login`. Ping me when done.
   Stop and wait.
2. **Must be a git repo.** Attribution is diff-based; there is no scope without
   one.
3. **Note a dirty tree** if reviewing a committed scope, so the user knows the
   working-tree changes aren't included.

## Step 1 — attribute the diff

```bash
python3 ~/.claude/skills/cross-review/scripts/attribute.py --repo "$REPO"
```

Scope flags (default is `--uncommitted`):

| Flag | Scope |
|---|---|
| `--uncommitted` | staged + unstaged + untracked (default) |
| `--base main` | merge-base of `main`..HEAD — the branch's work |
| `--commit SHA` | one commit |
| `--range A..B` | an explicit revision range |

Other flags: `--days N` (transcript lookback, default 30), `--all-projects`
(force-scan every Claude project dir), `--mixed both` (files both agents touched
go to *both* reviewers instead of the opposite-of-dominant one),
`--session-agent codex` (set when Codex is driving, so human code routes to
Claude).

**How attribution works**, strongest signal first:

1. **Git trailers** (committed scopes) — Claude Code stamps
   `Co-Authored-By: Claude … <noreply@anthropic.com>`. Codex stamps nothing, so
   a Codex-written commit is identified via transcripts, not trailers.
2. **Transcripts on disk** — `~/.claude/projects/<slug>/*.jsonl` (Edit/Write
   tool calls) and `~/.codex/sessions/**/rollout-*.jsonl` (`patch_apply_end`
   change maps, `apply_patch` envelopes, and shell redirect writes). Paths
   resolve against each session's `cwd`. Codex's record format has changed
   across versions, so all three forms are parsed.
3. **Nothing found** → `unknown`, routed as human.

Each file comes back with `author`, `confidence`, `reviewer`, and `evidence`.
**Show the user the attribution table before reviewing** — it's often the most
interesting output, and a wrong call there sends the diff to the wrong model.

## Step 2 — dispatch both reviewers

```bash
python3 ~/.claude/skills/cross-review/scripts/attribute.py --repo "$REPO" --json \
  | python3 ~/.claude/skills/cross-review/scripts/dispatch.py
```

This builds a per-slice diff, runs `codex exec --sandbox read-only` and
`claude -p --allowed-tools Read Grep Glob` in parallel — **each as a swarm of
lens-specific agents** — and merges their structured findings sorted by
severity. Add `--keep-raw` to retain raw reviewer output for debugging and
`--timeout N` (default 900s) for big diffs.

### The swarm — lenses, not one generalist

One generalist reviewer per side hits a breadth ceiling: it finds the loudest
defect in a file and moves on. So each side runs the **same diff** through
several agents that each carry a different question:

| Lens | Asks |
|---|---|
| `correctness` (default) | does this compute the wrong answer? boundaries, inverted conditions, state transitions, empty/null/negative inputs |
| `security` (default) | who can reach this with hostile input? authz, injection, timing-unsafe compares, secrets, traversal, missing limits |
| `concurrency-resources` (default) | unawaited promises, TOCTOU, mutation during iteration, leaked handles, missing cleanup on the error path, unbounded growth |
| `contracts` (opt-in) | do the two sides of each boundary agree on types, nullability, units, ordering? swallowed errors, half-written state, non-idempotent retries |

`--lenses a,b,c` picks the set; `--lenses none` runs the old single generalist
pass. Default is 3 lenses × 2 sides = **6 concurrent agents on one diff** —
that is the cost of the swarm, and `--lenses none` is the cheap mode for a small
or low-stakes diff. `agents_run` in the output says how many actually ran.

Findings are then **deduped across lenses**. Two findings merge when they are in
the same file within 3 lines, name ≥2 of the same code identifiers (backticked
spans, camelCase, snake_case — prose varies, symbol names don't), **and** their
defect kinds don't contradict. That last gate matters: every lens looking at one
broken function names the same symbols, so without it an unawaited promise, an
unhandled rejection, an unbounded fan-out and a missing authz check on the same
line collapse into one finding with four different fixes (observed, then fixed).
Merged findings carry `raised_by: N`, the lenses that saw it, and every other
description under `corroborating_summaries`. `raised` vs `after_dedupe` shows
how much overlap there was.

- **`raised_by > 1` is the swarm's strongest signal** — agents asking different
  questions converged on one defect. Lead with those and say so.
- **Always read `corroborating_summaries` on a merged finding.** Clustering is
  lexical and the defect-kind gate only recognises common kinds, so a *related
  but distinct* defect can still land in the same cluster. If a corroborating
  summary describes a different failure, split it back out and report it
  separately. Nothing is discarded — but nothing is verified either.

### Repo context — what the diff doesn't show

Reviewers also get a **usage pack** built alongside the diff: the symbols this
diff declares or changes, grepped for their call sites elsewhere in the repo
(`file:line`, capped at 12 symbols × 6 sites). This is the cheap local analogue
of Greptile's repo graph — a reviewer with the callers in hand checks whether
the change breaks them; a reviewer that has to go looking usually doesn't.
`--no-context` skips it.

Reviews take minutes on a real diff — **run this in the background and poll**
rather than blocking.

If a reviewer fails, its error lands in `errors` while the other's findings
still come through. Report partial results honestly; never present a one-sided
review as a full cross-review.

### Models — the thing that decides whether this is worth running

Two frontier reasoning models arguing about a diff is a real check. A mini-tier
model on either side still emits confident-sounding findings, so a downgrade is
invisible in the output — it just turns into noise you then have to verify. The
script therefore **pins models rather than inheriting CLI defaults**:

| Reviewer | Default | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Claude | `--model opus --effort high` | the alias resolves to the latest Opus, so it never goes stale; `claude -p` would otherwise follow whatever the user last picked in `/model` |
| Codex | `gpt-5.6-sol` at `-c model_reasoning_effort="high"` | the flagship coding model. A configured model is respected only if it is the **same generation or newer** and not a cheap tier |

The Codex floor is **generation-aware**, not just a name blocklist — a whole
generation is a bigger quality gap than any prompt tuning:

- `gpt-5.4`, `gpt-5.5` → upgraded (older generation than `gpt-5.6`)
- `gpt-5.6-luna`, anything `mini/nano/lite/flash/…` → upgraded (cheap tier)
- `gpt-5.6-terra`, `gpt-5.6-sol`, `gpt-5.7`, `gpt-6.x` → kept as configured

**Pinning the effort matters as much as pinning the model here: `gpt-5.6-sol`'s
own default reasoning level is `low`.** Asking the flagship for a review without
an explicit effort gets you its cheapest thinking. Sol and Terra also support
`xhigh`, `max`, and `ultra` above `high` — reach for `--codex-effort xhigh` on a
gnarly diff.

Overrides: `--codex-model` / `--claude-model`, `--codex-effort` /
`--claude-effort`. Use `--claude-model fable` for the hardest diffs. The resolved
model, effort, and where each came from are echoed to stderr at launch and
recorded in the output JSON under `reviewers` — **quote them in your report** so
a silent downgrade is visible.

When new models ship, update `CODEX_STRONG_DEFAULT` / `CODEX_MIN_GENERATION` at
the top of `dispatch.py`. To see what the installed CLI actually supports rather
than guessing: `strings -a /Applications/ChatGPT.app/Contents/Resources/codex |
rg -o 'gpt-5\.[0-9]+(-[a-z]+)?' | sort -u`, and the same dump carries each
model's `supported_reasoning_levels` and `context_window`.

## Step 3 — verify by execution

```bash
python3 ~/.claude/skills/cross-review/scripts/verify.py --repo "$REPO" --findings review.json
```

Each qualifying finding gets its **own disposable git worktree** (uncommitted
state applied, untracked files copied, `node_modules`/`.venv`/`vendor` symlinked
in) and its own agent, told to write a minimal reproduction, **run it**, and
return the command plus real output. Verdicts are `reproduced` / `refuted` /
`inconclusive`, written back onto each finding as a `verification` block with
`what_i_ran` and `observed`.

The verifier is the model that didn't write the code **and** isn't the one that
raised the finding, so a confabulated bug has to survive an independent attempt
to make it happen. Nothing touches the real repo — the worktrees are removed
afterwards.

Defaults: top 6 findings at medium+ severity and confidence (`--max`,
`--min-severity`, `--min-confidence`, `--all`). Anything skipped is announced on
stderr — **an unverified finding must never be reported as checked**.

Read the verdicts critically rather than trusting the label:

- `reproduced` with real output in `observed` — this is the strongest evidence
  the pipeline produces. Treat it as confirmed.
- `refuted` — believe it only if `what_i_ran` actually exercises the claimed
  path. A repro that stubbed away the interesting part refutes nothing. **Check
  the verdict against its own `observed` output**: a verifier that ran two
  variants and reports the passing one has refuted nothing. This is the observed
  failure mode — a real unawaited-promise bug came back `refuted` because a
  synchronously-resolving mock hid it, while the same run's timer-based variant
  printed the empty array that proves it. The prompt now forbids instant stubs
  for async claims, but read the evidence anyway.
- `inconclusive` — the claim is **unproven**, not "probably real". Say so.

`inconclusive` is the normal verdict for anything needing a live service, a
browser, or a full build, so expect it and fall back to Step 3b for those.

## Step 3b — verify by reading, when execution can't settle it

The findings are **claims from another model, not facts**. A reviewer that
didn't write the code also doesn't know the code's context, and cross-model
review produces confident-sounding false positives about intentional behavior.

For anything Step 3 left `inconclusive`, or skipped:

- Open the file and trace the actual code path; check the claimed failure
  scenario really occurs — inputs, state, ordering.
- Rule out the usual false positives: behavior guaranteed by a caller, an
  invariant enforced elsewhere, a deliberate choice the surrounding code makes,
  or an "unhandled" case that is genuinely unreachable.
- If you can settle it by running something yourself, do that instead — Step 3's
  cap and gates are budget decisions, not judgments about what's checkable.
- Drop anything you can't confirm. Say how many you dropped and why, and say
  which survivors were **reproduced by execution** versus confirmed by reading.
  Those are different strengths of evidence and the report must not blur them.

Note the asymmetry in what the reviewers themselves could do: `codex exec
--sandbox read-only` can run commands, while the Claude reviewer gets only
Read/Grep/Glob. Pass `--claude-bash` to give it command access too — useful on
a repo with a fast test suite, but it lets that subprocess run arbitrary
commands in the repo, so it is opt-in.

## Step 4 — fix and report

**Auto-fix** a finding only when **all** of these hold:

- the reviewer marked it `confidence: high`, **and**
- it was **`reproduced`** in Step 3, or you independently confirmed it yourself
  in Step 3b — an `inconclusive` verdict is not a confirmation, **and**
- the fix is local and unambiguous — a missing `await`, an off-by-one, a
  timing-unsafe comparison, an unchecked null. One obvious correct answer.

**Never auto-fix**: anything touching public API shape, schema/migrations, auth
or crypto policy, concurrency design, deletions of existing behavior, or
anything where two reasonable fixes exist. Those go to the user as open items
with a recommendation.

After applying fixes, **run the repo's tests/build/linter** if it has them, and
report the actual result. Show the user the diff of what you changed.

### Record the verdicts — this is what makes the next run better

Once you know what was real, write it back. Otherwise the same false positive
returns every run and you learn to skim the output:

```bash
echo '[{"file":"src/cache.py","line":9,"category":"correctness",
       "summary":"time.time() used for TTL","outcome":"dropped",
       "reason":"cache is advisory and process-local; monotonic not required"},
      {"file":"src/auth.ts","line":42,"category":"security",
       "summary":"token compared with ==","outcome":"fixed"}]' \
  | python3 ~/.claude/skills/cross-review/scripts/record.py --repo "$REPO"
```

`outcome` is `dropped` (false positive), `confirmed`, or `fixed`. Record **every**
finding you adjudicated, dropped ones especially — a rejection without a `reason`
is nearly worthless, since the next reviewer can't tell whether the code changed.

`verify.py` output can be piped straight in: a `reproduced` verdict records as
`confirmed` and a `refuted` one as `dropped`, both with the observed output as
the reason. `inconclusive` is skipped — never let an unproven claim enter the
memory as adjudicated.

```bash
python3 …/verify.py --repo "$REPO" --findings review.json \
  | python3 …/record.py --repo "$REPO"
```

Stored per repo under `~/.claude/skills/cross-review/state/`, replayed into the
next review's prompt as "already rejected, don't raise again" plus "this repo has
really had these bugs, check for recurrences". `record.py --show` inspects it,
`--forget N` prunes recent dismissals, `dispatch.py --no-memory` ignores it for
one run. When a run starts with stored memory, dispatch says so on stderr —
mention it in the report, because a suppressed finding is invisible otherwise.

Report in this shape:

```
Reviewers:    codex gpt-5.4 (high) · claude opus (high) · 6 agents, 3 lenses
Attribution:  5 files Claude → Codex reviewed · 3 files Codex → Claude reviewed
Findings:     9 raised → 7 after dedupe · 2 raised by 2 lenses independently
Verification: 4 reproduced by execution · 2 refuted · 1 inconclusive (read instead)
Memory:       3 previously-dismissed findings suppressed this run

FIXED
  src/db.ts:17    ×2  [high]  unawaited promise (correctness + concurrency lenses
                              independently) — REPRODUCED: repro printed [] where
                              2 rows expected. Added await; tests pass.
OPEN
  src/auth.ts:42      [high]  token compared with == (timing-unsafe)
                              confirmed by reading (not executed — timing needs a
                              statistical harness)
                              → recommend crypto.timingSafeEqual; needs your call
                              on the encoding
DROPPED
  src/cli.ts:88               REFUTED by execution: called with null, returned the
                              default instead of throwing (see cli.ts:61 guard)
```

Say how each survivor was established — **reproduced by execution** or
**confirmed by reading**. They are not the same evidence and the reader can't
tell them apart unless you do.

Attribute honestly: say which model raised each finding, and be explicit that
you fixed some and left others. If both reviewers flagged the same defect
independently, say so — that agreement is a strong signal.

## Notes and limits

- **Transcripts outrank commit trailers.** A trailer says "an agent co-authored
  this commit"; a transcript names the exact file. So when Codex writes a file
  and Claude commits it, the file is still Codex's — the common case when you
  ask one agent to commit another's work.
- **Committed attribution is commit-level, not line-level.** A file in a
  Claude-stamped commit is treated as Claude's, even if a human hand-edited part
  of it. `evidence` flags when a file was modified well after the last agent
  edit.
- **Codex leaves no commit trailer**, so committed Codex work is only detectable
  while its rollout is inside the `--days` window. Widen `--days` for older work.
- **Transcripts are the ground truth for uncommitted code.** If the user cleared
  `~/.claude/projects` or `~/.codex/sessions`, everything reads as `unknown` and
  routes to Codex by default. Say so rather than silently defaulting.
- The first run may take ~5s if it has to widen the transcript search; matching
  runs inside the repo are much faster.
- `codex exec review --uncommitted` (Codex's own built-in reviewer) is a good
  manual escape hatch for a deeper whole-diff pass when everything routes to
  Codex anyway.

content.text:
Two settled by reading while verification runs:

- **`AppState.swift:575` — confirmed.** `BridgeClient` fires the completion for *any* response with a matching id, including `ok:false`, with `result` defaulting to `[:]` (BridgeClient.swift:176-186). So a transient `transcript_error` reads as `text: ""` and blanks the card. That was harmless when the transcript was only the on-demand viewer; it isn't now that it's the card's primary content.
- **`AppState.swift:641` — confirmed.** `cardText` prefers `claudeCardText` with no check on the surface's *current* kind, so a terminal where Claude has exited keeps rendering the old conversation with fresh shell output composed underneath it.

Every verified finding reproduced — nothing was refuted, which is itself worth noting: Codex's claims held up under an independent attempt to make them happen.

**FIXED — reproduced by execution (6)**

- `transcript.go:194` **[high]** A surface's store record outlives the session that wrote it, so after SessionEnd cleared the pointer, a surface running session B was served ended session A *indefinitely*. Repro printed `source="hook_store_surface" sessionID=aaaaaaaa…` while `checkpoint_id=bbbbbbbb…`. Checkpoint strategies now outrank every surface-keyed lookup.
- `transcript.go:198` An inconsistent active pointer served **another surface's conversation** — the exact invariant the code comments claim. Repro: surface A asked for its checkpoint and got surface B's session. The pointer and record must now agree on the surface.
- `hookstore.go:185` Store paths followed symlinks and weren't tied to the claimed session — repro read `SECRET: prod db password is hunter2` through a redirect. Paths now resolve through symlinks and must still be named `<sessionID>.jsonl`; the directory stays free so `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` relocation still works (verified all 34 real records satisfy this).
- `transcript.go:163` My cache key change made growth unbounded: repro pinned **897 MiB** over 2000 client-chosen `max_messages` values, and retained 500 deleted transcripts. Now capped at 8 entries.
- `AppState.swift:567` ×2 lenses — the 15s timeout cleared whichever request held the mark, killing a live spinner and letting two RPCs stack. Per-request generation token.
- `AppState.swift:603` ×2 lenses — out-of-order detached trims pinned older text under a *newer* fingerprint, which `unchanged` then preserved forever. Applied-seq guard; fingerprint now stamped with the text it describes.

**FIXED — confirmed by reading (5)**: RPC errors blanking the card (`BridgeClient.swift:176-186` fires completions for `ok:false` with an empty result); `cardText` ignoring the surface's current kind; two unbounded reads trusting a pre-open stat; transcript state released on explicit close.

**DROPPED (1)**: tool-argument summaries carrying secrets — the transcript already contains whatever was typed, and showing it on the paired phone is the feature. Recorded with that reason so it doesn't resurface.
